thread.title_full: Ethiopia Expels Eritrean Diplomats Amid Renewed Northern Fighting

author: Ahmed Ibrahim World Editor
title: Ethiopia Expels Eritrean Diplomats Amid Renewed Northern Fighting
text:
Ethiopia ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave Addis Ababa within 48 hours and closed its embassy in Asmara on October 1, 2026, as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia triggered a sharp diplomatic rupture and tit-for-tat expulsions across the Horn of Africa.
The sudden diplomatic collapse marks a severe downturn in relations between two neighbors whose 2018 rapprochement once earned international praise. Federal forces and an armed opposition alliance have been clashing across several northern fronts since late September, reviving fears of a wider conflict mirroring the devastating 2020–2022 civil war.
Expulsions and Embassy Closures in Addis Ababa and Asmara
Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry initiated the cascade of measures on Thursday by announcing the closure of its embassy in the Eritrean capital. The government stated the shutdown occurred in response to Eritrea’s direct and indirect acts of hostility and belligerence against Ethiopia. Simultaneously, Addis Ababa declared 10 Eritrean diplomatic personnel — including the charge d’affaires and representatives accredited to the African Union — unwanted persons.
The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry asserted that the targeted diplomats had engaged in involvement in activities that pose a direct threat to Ethiopia’s national security, giving them a 48-hour deadline to exit the country.
Eritrea swiftly condemned the directive. In a statement reported by international news agencies, Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel explained that removing all diplomatic staff effectively shuttered the Eritrean embassy in Ethiopia’s capital, leaving Asmara no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia with all the negative corollaries that this entails.
The historical context of these ties dates back decades. Following the 1998–2000 border war and decades of hostility, Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki restored relations in 2018 after an armed independence struggle, led by Eritrea’s current president, had secured independence in 1993.
The rapprochement that culminated in Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed receiving the Nobel Peace Prize saw Ethiopia’s embassy in Eritrea reopened in 2018. During the 2020–2022 Tigray war, Eritrean forces entered Tigray alongside Ethiopian federal forces. However, Eritrea was not a party to the Pretoria Peace Agreement that ended the fighting in November 2022, and relations between the neighbors quickly soured amid disagreements surrounding regional security and Ethiopia’s pursuit of direct sea access for landlocked Ethiopia.
Explosions in the Ethiopian Capital and the Tigray Conflict Backdrop
The diplomatic crisis unfolded against a backdrop of acute security alarms in Addis Ababa. An intelligence official and diplomatic sources confirmed that three blasts occurred in three different locations in the capital overnight, including near defense headquarters, prompting sirens and heightened drone flight restrictions.
Federal authorities have accused Eritrea, Sudan, and Egypt of backing an opposition coalition led by the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). This alliance has launched major assaults against federal forces, with medical organizations registering hundreds of wounded patients at hospitals in Korem, Alamata, and Shire. Doctors Without Borders reported registering more than 420 wounded at Korem and Alamata hospitals and more than 300 at Shire in western Tigray.
Cairo Reciprocates as Diplomatic Fallout Widens to Egypt
The diplomatic fallout quickly drew in Cairo as Ethiopia ordered an Egyptian diplomatic staff member to leave the country within 48 hours. The Ethiopian Foreign Ministry formally notified the Egyptian Embassy that Ahmed Moharam Ahmed Soliman was persona non grata.
Egypt responded promptly under the principle of diplomatic reciprocity. State-affiliated media reported that Cairo declared an Ethiopian embassy counselor, identified as Egazi Emelo Borougi, persona non grata with a matching 48-hour departure deadline.
The Ethiopian side has a history of attributing its failures in managing its internal affairs and its successive crises to alleged foreign interference, thereby concealing its ongoing problems.
A senior Egyptian official, via MENA
Regional Appeals for Restraint Amid Horn of Africa Uncertainty
As diplomatic channels collapse, the African Union Commission has called for maximum restraint among Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Egypt. The commission warned against actions that could further destabilize the Horn of Africa, where overlapping security crises and long-standing disputes over Nile water resources and maritime access already strain regional stability.
While international observers watch for further escalation, the immediate question remains whether the rupture between Addis Ababa and Asmara will stay contained to the diplomatic sphere or ignite a wider interstate military confrontation.
